name: Beth Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Len's garage on the industrial estate by half seven, kettle on, then whatever's on the board. Mostly older cars, brakes, exhausts, suspension, the odd clutch that Len does while I hold the light. I like the smell of it, honestly, and I like when a rattle that's been driving someone mad for a month just stops. What wears me out is the diagnostic tablet, because I'm slow on it and Len has to come over and press the right buttons.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's the money like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Coming up three years, after I left the cafe. I'm on the bottom rate, and after rent and my half of the bills with Sam, my partner, there's maybe forty quid left most months. Sam picks at a warehouse out by the ring road. There are two other garages in town and neither of them is hiring, so if Len's goes, I'm basically back to making coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say told you so, to be honest. Everyone was going on about it and it turned out to be another gadget. At work I'd say the cars still need someone under them, and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my problems were never AI anyway. Len is sixty-three and talks about packing in every winter, and the big dealer in town is doing cheap service deals that take our regulars. I've got under a month of rent saved, so one bad month at the garage and I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and try to get faster on brakes so Len trusts me with more jobs on my own. I'd stop buying lunch at the van and bring sandwiches, because that's about fifteen quid a week. Maybe ask Len straight out what his plan is for retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not relieved, exactly. More like the same knot in my stomach I've had since I started. It's a small garage with one old man holding it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Len about his plans. What stops you asking now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear of the answer, mostly. If he says two years, I've got to start looking, and there's nothing to look at. So I just don't ask, and I hold the torch and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the garage did close, what's the first thing that would go at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam can't cover the flat on warehouse money alone. My half of the rent goes straight away, and we'd be moving back in with my mum. That's the bit that keeps me up, not robots.

say: AI turned out to be **another gadget**, and cars still need someone underneath them.
I'd tell people at work that **nothing changes** for mechanics like us.
think: My real worry is **Len retiring**, not AI, and the big dealer taking our regulars.
With **under a month** of rent saved, one slow month at the garage puts me in trouble.
do: **Speed up** on brake jobs so Len lets me work alone more often.
**Bring sandwiches** instead of buying lunch, saving about fifteen pounds a week.
Think about asking Len his **retirement plan**, though I keep putting it off.
feel: The **same knot** in my stomach I've carried since I started at the garage.
S0.quote: My half of the rent goes straight away, and we'd be moving back in with my mum. That's the bit that keeps me up, not robots.
fieldNote: Beth's anxiety is **already there** before AI: an ageing owner, a cheap dealer rival, almost no savings.
She avoids asking her boss about retirement because the answer could force a job hunt she **can't face**.
Her fallback is moving in with her mother, which she describes as the **real nightmare**.

steps.text: Get faster on brake jobs so Len trusts her alone
Bring sandwiches instead of buying lunch from the van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the dealers and the big chains that'll go mad for it, not little places like Len's. Online I'd probably share something about how the people building this should have to pay for retraining. Somebody should be making them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the bit that worries me is the booking and the parts. Len's daughter does the phones and the parts ordering two days a week, and if software does that, it's one less wage, fine. But if the chains get cheaper because their computer books and orders everything, our regulars go there, and that's my job gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work. I'm not going to go on some course about AI, I'm useless at that stuff and I'd just be wasting money I haven't got. I might look at joining the motor trades union, because if things shift, I'd rather have someone in my corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, really. Like everyone keeps moving the floor and I'm still trying to learn where the bolts go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip a course. What if Len asked you to learn the new booking software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, grumbling, because he asked. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it, same as the tablet. I've always been better with my hands than a screen, that's why I'm here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the garage would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Len's daughter, Kerry, because the phones and parts are exactly what the card said. Then me, because I'm the cheapest to lose and the slowest. My boss Len would keep himself, obviously.

say: The **big chains** will grab AI first, not small places like Len's garage.
The firms building AI should **pay for retraining**, and someone should make them.
think: Chains with software doing **booking and parts** could get cheaper and pull our regulars away.
I'm the **cheapest and slowest** at the garage, so I'd be the first one let go.
do: **Skip paid courses** on AI, because I can't afford them and I'm slow on screens.
Look into joining the **motor trades union** so someone has my back.
feel: **Tired**, like the floor keeps moving while I'm still learning the basics.
S1.quote: I'm the cheapest to lose and the slowest. My boss Len would keep himself, obviously.
fieldNote: Beth sees the threat coming through **price competition** from chains, not robots in her own bay.
Her progressive outlook shows in wanting AI firms to **fund retraining** and in turning to a union.
She'd only learn software if her boss asked, and admits she'd **resent it**.

steps.text: Keep working full days at Len's garage and learn more repairs
Ask about joining the motor trades union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry, out loud. I'd be posting that the government let this happen with no plan for people like me. At work I'd probably say at least they can't fix a car yet, which is true for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got three years, maybe. The diagnostic and quoting side goes in 2028, and that's the bit I'm already bad at. Then by 2031 there's a robot that can do a brake job, and I'll be thirty-two with no savings and nothing else I'm trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably just keep working until it stops, because I don't know what else to do. I'd sign up to the union for sure, and go to whatever protest or meeting there is about it. I'd start putting something away every week, even twenty quid, so there's something when it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years. What would you want to have done by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have a bit of money saved and maybe know someone in a different line of work. Sam talks about the care home on the estate always needing people, and I'd look at that. People will still want a person to hold their hand, surely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're both in trouble, because the warehouse goes before the garage. I'd say we can't be the people with nothing at the end of this. Then we'd probably sit there and not know what to do.

say: The **government let this happen** with no plan for people like me.
At work I'd say robots **can't fix a car** yet, which buys a few years.
think: Diagnostics and quoting go in **2028**, and those are the parts I'm already worst at.
By **2031** I'd be thirty-two, with no savings and no other trade.
do: **Join the union** and turn up to any meetings or protests about it.
Put away **twenty pounds a week** so there's something when the garage work goes.
Keep working at the garage **until it stops**, because I don't have another plan.
feel: **Sick**, like waiting for a letter I know is coming.
S2.quote: By 2031 there's a robot that can do a brake job, and I'll be thirty-two with no savings and nothing else I'm trained for.
fieldNote: Beth grasps the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots, and treats it as borrowed time.
Both household incomes are exposed; she expects Sam's **warehouse job** to go first.
Her only fallback idea is **care work**, raised by her partner rather than herself.

steps.text: Sign up to the union and attend meetings on AI job losses
Put twenty pounds a week into a savings jar
Keep doing brake and exhaust jobs at Len's until work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws now, while there's time. Like I said with the fast one, somebody has to make the companies pay for what they're doing. I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years sounds like more time, but I know me. I'd waste three of them hoping it doesn't happen. Then in 2031 the screen side goes, and 2034 the robots, and I'd be thirty-five and still at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union, properly this time, not just sign up. I'd try to save, but on my wage it's tiny. I might ask Len if I could do my vehicle inspection certificate, because at least then I'm worth a bit more to someone for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit ashamed, because I can see myself doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd waste the time. What would get you to actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody I trust going first, I think. If someone at the union said here's a free course and here's a job at the end, I'd go. I won't spend my own money gambling on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out with Sam's mates on a Friday, which is the only fun we have. Then the car I'm doing up in Len's back yard, which kills me. I'd sell it for parts.

say: We need **laws now**, while there's time, so companies pay for the damage.
I'd sign **every petition** going about it.
think: I'd likely **waste three years** hoping it doesn't happen.
By **2034** I'd be thirty-five and still on the bottom rung.
do: Get **properly involved** in the union instead of just signing up.
Ask Len about doing the **vehicle inspection certificate** to be worth more for a few years.
Sell the **project car** for parts if money gets tighter.
feel: **Uneasy** and a little ashamed, because I can picture myself doing nothing.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like more time, but I know me. I'd waste three of them hoping it doesn't happen.
fieldNote: Beth is unusually **honest about inertia**; more time doesn't help someone who won't move alone.
She'd only retrain if a **trusted body** offered a free course with a job at the end.
Losing her **project car** clearly hurts more than she lets on.

steps.text: Go to union branch meetings regularly, not just pay dues
Ask Len to put her through the vehicle inspection certificate
Sell the project car in Len's yard for parts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough that nobody has an excuse. The government should be setting up proper retraining now, paid for by the companies. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is my whole thirties. I could actually learn something in that time, even slow like me. Robots in 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine, and that's late but not finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the inspection certificate in the first couple of years. I'd keep saving a bit, maybe start a small pot with Sam for a deposit somewhere cheaper. And I'd keep pushing the union to get training out of the employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, because the money's still thin and Len's still old. But there's a bit of room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said care work. Is that still in your head with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at the end, yeah. But with ten years I'd rather stay around cars, maybe checking what the robots did, if that's a job. I don't know if it will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the first step, given how you said you'd waste time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Len making training part of the job, honestly. If training is on the rota, I'll do it. If it's up to me on a Sunday night, I won't.

say: Ten years is **long enough** that nobody has an excuse for doing nothing.
Companies should **pay for retraining** now, organised by the government.
think: Ten years is **my whole thirties**, enough to learn something even at my pace.
By **2039** I'd be thirty-nine, which is late but not finished.
do: Take the **inspection certificate** in the first couple of years.
Start a **small savings pot** with Sam toward a cheaper place.
Keep pushing the **union** to win training from employers.
feel: Still **worried** about thin money and Len's age, but with some room to breathe.
S4.quote: If training is on the rota, I'll do it. If it's up to me on a Sunday night, I won't.
fieldNote: The longer runway lowers her alarm, but **Len's age** and thin savings keep her anxious.
She imagines a future job **checking robot work**, while admitting she doesn't know if it'll exist.
Change only happens for Beth when **someone else** builds it into her working week.

steps.text: Complete the vehicle inspection certificate within two years
Open a joint savings pot with Sam toward a cheaper flat
Push the union branch to get employer-funded training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. That one leaves me thirty-two with no trade and no money, and Sam's job gone first. What would help is a training place that pays you while you learn, because I can't learn for free, I've got rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I don't hate change, I just can't afford to get it wrong. When you've got forty quid at the end of the month, it's maths. People think resisting is being stubborn, but it isn't.

headlineQuote: I don't hate change, I just can't afford to get it wrong. When you've got forty quid at the end of the month, it's maths.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** junior mechanic at a small garage owned by Len, who is sixty-three.
She has **under a month** saved, shares rent with Sam, and sees few other garages hiring.
She avoids screens and AI tools and calls her caution **simple maths**, not stubbornness.
Her fear grows from **anxious to alarmed** as AGI comes faster, easing slightly with ten years.
She leans on the **union** and petitions, wanting AI companies to fund retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving her thirty-two with no trade, no savings and Sam's warehouse job gone.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** that covers rent while she learns, organised by someone she trusts.
